entries.s: ADFGVX cipher — Germany's WWI field cipher fusing a 6x6 Polybius square with keyed columnar transposition. Broken by Georges Painvin in June 1918.
ADFGX cipher — March 1918 German field cipher pairing a 5x5 Polybius square with keyed columnar transposition. Broken by Painvin three months later.
Aeneas Tacticus (~350 BCE) — the Greek general who wrote the world's earliest surviving manual on military communications, including the synchronized water-clock signaling code.
AES (2001) — the cipher that encrypts the modern world; chosen by open competition, scrutinised for two decades, still without a practical attack.
The affine cipher — a single linear formula E(x)=a·x+b mod 26 that generalises Caesar (a=1) and Atbash (a=25, b=25). Just 312 keys; trivially broken.

Agnes Meyer Driscoll was the U.S. Navy's chief cryptanalyst for three decades, breaking Japanese naval codes and training generations of American codebreakers. Known as 'Miss Aggie' and 'Madame X', she was the most formidable cryptanalyst in prewar America.
Alberti cipher disk — Leon Battista Alberti's 1467 rotating disk, the first true polyalphabetic device and the tool that began the cipher revolution.
Ethiopian Orthodox monasteries used syllabary-based substitution ciphers in Ge'ez script to protect sacred texts and inter-monastery communications from the 14th century onward.
9th-century Abbasid Baghdad — al-Kindi's Risalah and the codebooks of the Arab cryptographic golden age, where frequency analysis was born.

entries.b: Secure for its time · obsoleted by frequency analysis
entries.s: Matteo and Marcello Argenti served as papal cryptanalysts to seven popes. Their Trattato in Cifra codified the homophonic-nomenclator pattern that dominated European diplomacy for two centuries.
g: secure for its time · obsoleted by frequency analysis

entries.s: The book cipher Benedict Arnold and Major John André used to plot the surrender of West Point. Each plaintext word located in a shared book (Blackstone’s Commentaries) and transmitted as the triple page.line.word.
Atbash — the ancient Hebrew reflection cipher (A<->Z, B<->Y, C<->X), self-inverse and used in the Book of Jeremiah (25:26, 51:41) for SHESHACH.
Autokey (1586) — Vigenère's self-extending key, the message becomes its own key. Effectively unbreakable until Friedman's 1920s statistical attack.
Babington Plot nomenclator (1586) — the cipher that condemned Mary, Queen of Scots, broken in days by Walsingham's cryptographer Thomas Phelippes.
The four notes B♭ – A – C – B♮ spell 'BACH' in German musical notation — a self-signature Bach embedded in his final unfinished fugue.
Bacon's bilateral cipher (1605) — Francis Bacon's 5-bit binary code that hides letters inside a two-typeface carrier, the direct ancestor of ASCII.
Bazeries cylinder cipher — Etienne Bazeries' 1898 wheel cipher with 20 alphabet disks, an evolution later adopted by the US Army as the M-94 in 1922.
Beale ciphers (~1820) — three book ciphers said to lead to a Virginia treasure. Only #2 was solved (Declaration of Independence key); #1 and #3 unsolved.
Beaufort cipher (1857) — Sir Francis Beaufort's reciprocal Vigenère variant where encrypt and decrypt are the same operation. Broken by Kasiski examination.

Swedish mathematician Arne Beurling broke the German Siemens T52 Geheimschreiber cipher in two weeks in 1940 — an achievement described by NSA historians as perhaps the greatest individual cryptanalytic feat in history.

The Bible Code — equidistant letter sequences (ELS) claimed to hide prophecies in the Hebrew scriptures. A rigorous statistical refutation by McKay et al. (1999) showed the same method finds identical 'predictions' in War and Peace and Moby-Dick.
Bifid cipher (1901) — Felix Delastelle's fractionation cipher that splits Polybius coordinates, transposes them across a period, and recombines.

Bill Tutte was a Cambridge mathematician who reconstructed the complete logical structure of the Lorenz SZ40 cipher machine from ciphertext alone — without ever seeing the machine — enabling the creation of Colossus, the world's first programmable electronic computer.

Bletchley Park (Station X) was the British WWII signals intelligence headquarters where 10,000 people broke Enigma, Lorenz, and dozens of other Axis ciphers — arguably shortening the war by two years.

entries.b: Secure if the book is unguessable; broken otherwise
entries.s: Book Cipher (18th c.) — if both correspondents share the same book, the book itself is the key. Used by Benedict Arnold, Aaron Burr, and Beale.
g: secure if the book is unguessable; broken otherwise

entries.t: Cabinet Noir — Black Chambers of Europe
entries.s: The European Black Chambers (cabinets noirs) were government departments that intercepted, deciphered, and resealed diplomatic mail from the 16th through 19th centuries — proto-signals-intelligence agencies.
Caesar cipher — the simplest substitution cipher, used by Julius Caesar around 58 BC with a shift of 3. Broken by Al-Kindi's frequency analysis circa 850 AD.
Girolamo Cardano's 1550 autokey — prime the keystream with a single seed letter, then continue it with the plaintext itself. The first published self-keying scheme.
Girolamo Cardano's 1550 grille — a card with cut-out windows. Write the secret through the windows; fill the rest with innocuous text; the recipient overlays an identical grille to read.
Chaocipher (1918) — John F. Byrne's two-disk dynamic cipher that permutes both alphabets after every character. Unsolved for 90 years until Rubin's 2010 break.
Ernesto 'Che' Guevara used a modified VIC straddling-checkerboard cipher for guerrilla communications in Bolivia and the Congo, 1956–1967.

The 1881 Chinese Telegraph Code mapped 7,000+ Chinese characters to 4-digit code groups so they could ride the same Morse-style telegraph network as the Latin alphabet — and was super-enciphered for diplomatic and military traffic in the 20th century.

An anonymous 2012–2014 internet recruitment puzzle that combined steganography, classical ciphers, GPS coordinates on physical posters, and a copy of the Liber Primus hand-illustrated in glyphic runes.
Columnar transposition — write plaintext under a keyword, then read columns in keyword order. Broken by Friedman-era multiple-anagram methods in the 1920s.

Commercial telegraph codebooks (ABC Code, Bentley’s, Lieber’s) were the workhorses of Victorian and Edwardian global business. Each English word or phrase mapped to a 5-letter pronounceable codeword — cheaper, denser, and incidentally a layer of confidentiality.
Confederate Vigenère (1861-1865) — the brass cipher disk used by Confederate officers, broken in 1863 once the three repeating field keys were recovered.
Copiale Cipher — the 105-page 18th-century Oculist Order manuscript with homophonic substitution. Broken in 2011 by Knight, Megyesi, and Schaefer using HMM.

Major Benjamin Tallmadge’s 1779 codebook for George Washington’s Culper Spy Ring. Roughly 750 numbered entries covering people, places, military terms, and common words — used by Abraham Woodhull and Robert Townsend on British-occupied Long Island and Manhattan.
Dan Brown's 2003 thriller made cryptography mainstream — Atbash, the Fibonacci sequence, and anagrams as plot devices that introduced millions to cipher thinking.
A 1939 textbook 'cryptogram for the student' that the author himself later admitted he had forgotten how to solve.
The fictional stick-figure cipher Sherlock Holmes solves in The Adventure of the Dancing Men (1903) — a frequency-analysis primer disguised as a Strand magazine story.
DES (1977) — the first public, government-standardised cipher; broken by EFF Deep Crack in 1998 and the spark of modern academic cryptanalysis.
The US Army Special Forces one-time pad field system (1960s–1990s) — trigraph-based OTP cards issued to Green Berets in Vietnam.
Dictionary code — the Civil War book cipher that encodes each word as page-line-word triplets keyed to a shared dictionary, immune to frequency attacks.
Diffie-Hellman (1976) — two strangers create a shared secret over an open wire, ending three thousand years of must-meet-first cryptography.
Alfred Dillwyn "Dilly" Knox was the British codebreaker who solved the Enigma wiring before Turing, broke the Abwehr Enigma, and was the first to crack the Italian commercial Enigma variant.
Dorabella Cipher (1897) — Edward Elgar's 1897 cryptogram — 87 squiggles that have resisted every attempt since. Hall XII of The Cipher Museum.
Double transposition — apply columnar transposition twice with two keys. The WWII Allied workhorse, considered unbreakable until Lasry et al. (2013).
Elonka Dunin is a game designer, cryptographer, and the foremost public authority on unsolved ciphers — the creator of the definitive list of famous unsolved codes and an expert on Kryptos.
The Khnumhotep II tomb inscription (~1900 BCE) — the world's earliest surviving instance of a deliberate substitution cipher, using unusual hieroglyph variants.

Elizebeth Smith Friedman was America's first female professional cryptanalyst, who broke rum-runner codes during Prohibition, exposed Nazi spy networks in South America, and laid the foundations for what became the NSA.
Enigma (1923) — the German rotor cipher securing Wehrmacht and Kriegsmarine traffic. Broken by Polish mathematician Marian Rejewski in 1932.
The Soviet Cold-War rotor machine. Ten rotors, half stepping forward and half backward, plus a punch-card key sheet — the answer to every weakness Soviet analysts saw in Enigma.
American enslaved workers used field hollers, work songs, and coded idiom as covert communication — "Follow the Drinking Gourd" encoding an escape route along the Underground Railroad.
Four-Square cipher (1902) — Delastelle's digram cipher using two keyed and two standard 5x5 squares. Disrupts Playfair frequencies but breaks to digrams.
Fractionated Morse — converts text to Morse, regroups dots, dashes, and separators in trigrams, then substitutes via a keyed alphabet. Broken by trigram stats.
The geometric pigpen alphabet — fragments of grids and X-shapes — used by Freemasons, Rosicrucians, and the Hellfire Club from the 17th century onwards as a fraternal cipher and ritual marker.

entries.t: The GCHQ Trio — Ellis, Cocks, and Williamson
entries.s: James Ellis, Clifford Cocks, and Malcolm Williamson of GCHQ independently invented public-key cryptography in 1970–1973 — but their work remained classified until 1997, four years after Diffie, Hellman, and Rivest had received public credit.

The Siemens T52 “Sturgeon” — a German WWII teleprinter cipher with ten irregularly-clocked wheels feeding an additive keystream and a per-character permutation. Broken by Arne Beurling and the Swedish FRA in summer 1940.
Edgar Allan Poe's 1843 short story The Gold-Bug — the first widely read piece of fiction to teach cryptanalysis, complete with a worked decipherment of a buried-treasure cryptogram.

The Disney animated series Gravity Falls (2012–2016) hid a different cipher in every episode's credits — Caesar, Atbash, A1Z26 numeric, Vigenère — teaching real cryptography to a generation of children.
Great Cipher of Louis XIV (1626) — the Rossignol father-and-son syllabic nomenclator with delete-previous-letter traps. Broken by Bazeries in 1893.
Gronsfeld cipher (1655) — a Vigenère variant restricted to numeric keys (0-9), making it field-portable but with a smaller key space that falls fast to Kasiski.
Hill cipher (1929) — Lester S. Hill's matrix-based polygraphic cipher, first to apply linear algebra to encryption. Broken by known-plaintext (mod-26 system).
Histiaeus of Miletus (~499 BCE) — the Greek tyrant who tattooed a secret revolt order on a slave's shaved scalp, then waited for the hair to regrow before sending him.
Homophonic substitution (1400s) — replace each letter with one of several numeric codes to flatten frequencies. Defeated Mary in 1586; Great Cipher in 1893.
The Provisional IRA used book ciphers for encrypted communications between active service units and the Army Council — decoded when the FBI seized key material.
Jefferson disk cipher (1795) — Thomas Jefferson's 36-disk wheel cipher, rediscovered and adopted by the US Army as the M-94 in 1922. Solved by the late 20th c.
JN-25 (1939-1945) - the Imperial Japanese Navy's superenciphered codebook system broken by Station HYPO and central to Midway intelligence.
Joan Clarke was a Bletchley Park cryptanalyst who worked in Hut 8 alongside Alan Turing, making crucial contributions to breaking the Naval Enigma and to the development of the Bombe.
The Joseon Dynasty (1392–1897) Korean royal court used a cipher based on I Ching hexagram pairings to protect palace communications and diplomatic dispatches.
David Kahn's 1967 masterwork The Codebreakers was the first comprehensive history of cryptography — a book so thorough that the NSA tried to suppress its publication.
The Mlecchita Vikalpa cipher from Vatsyayana's Kama Sutra (~400 CE) — a paired-letter substitution taught to lovers as one of the 64 arts.
Auguste Kerckhoffs's 1883 principle — 'A cipher should be secure even if everything about the system, except the key, is public knowledge' — is the bedrock of modern cryptographic design.
The KL-7 (ADONIS) was NATO’s standard cipher machine from 1952 to 1968. Eight rotors, seven of which stepped, on a re-entrant alphabet. Compromised by John Walker, not by cryptanalysis.
Alexander von Kryha’s 1924 pocket cipher — a clockwork-driven mixed alphabet wheel sold to banks and diplomats as unbreakable, then broken in two hours by William Friedman.

Alternate-reality games — from The Beast (2001) to Year Zero (2007) and beyond — built on the assumption that players will recognise, transcribe, and crack classical ciphers across forums, phone calls, and physical artifacts.
Kryptos (1990) — Jim Sanborn's CIA-courtyard sculpture in four sections. K1, K2, K3 solved by 1999 (keyed Vigenère and transposition); K4 still unsolved.

George Lasry is a computational cryptographer who has solved more historically unsolved cipher manuscripts in the past decade than anyone alive — including the Copiale Cipher and multiple Zodiac Killer messages.
The commercial telegraph boom of 1870–1940 spawned a rich family of Latin American codebooks — from the Código Comercial Mexicano to the Código Telegráfico Argentino — that shaped 20th-century trade.

Leo Marks was the SOE's head of cryptography in WWII, who replaced vulnerable poem codes with one-time pads for field agents, dramatically reducing agent capture rates. He wrote the poem 'The Life That I Have' for agent Violette Szabo.
Lorenz SZ40 cipher (1940) — the German High Command teleprinter cipher with twelve pin-wheels. Broken by Bill Tutte in 1942; industrialised by Colossus in 1944.
The M-94 (Army) and CSP-488 (Navy) — 25 brass disks on a spindle, each carrying a mixed alphabet. Jefferson’s 1795 idea, mass-produced for WWI tactical traffic and used into 1942.
M-209 cipher machine (1940) — the US Army's portable Hagelin C-38 with six co-prime pin-wheels and a 27-bar lug cage. Broken in the field in WWII.

entries.t: Mary Queen of Scots — The Castelnau Letters
entries.s: The 1586 Castelnau letters by Mary Queen of Scots — a 50,000-character cipher solved by George Lasry, Beáta Megyesi, and Satoshi Tomokiyo in 2022, revealing undocumented French diplomatic intelligence.

Mavis Batey (née Lever) was a Bletchley Park cryptanalyst who broke the Italian naval Enigma in 1941, providing the intelligence behind the Battle of Cape Matapan — the Royal Navy's greatest WWII Mediterranean victory.
Two handwritten notes found in the pockets of murder victim Ricky McCormick in 1999 — declared 'unbreakable' by the FBI's Cryptanalysis and Racketeering Records Unit in 2011.

The microdot — a photograph reduced to the size of a typographic period — was the most effective covert communication tool of the 20th century, used by the Abwehr, KGB, and CIA from WWII through the Cold War.
An annual three-day puzzle marathon at MIT (since 1981) where teams solve dozens of layered cryptographic, linguistic, and lateral-thinking puzzles to find a hidden coin somewhere on campus.
Monoalphabetic substitution — replace each letter with a fixed substitute. Foundation of all substitution ciphers; broken by Al-Kindi's frequency analysis ~850.
International Morse code — the dot-dash telegraph alphabet that made the wired world possible and provided the carrier signal for a century of military and amateur ciphers.
The 2004 Disney film National Treasure sent audiences hunting for cipher clues on the US dollar bill, the Liberty Bell, and Independence Hall — all real historical sites.
Navajo Code (1942-1945) — a constructed military vocabulary spoken by 420 Marine Code Talkers. Never broken in wartime; declassified in 1968 after long use.
Nihilist cipher (1880s) — the Russian revolutionary classic adding Polybius numbers to a repeating keyword's Polybius numbers (mod 100). Broken early 1900s.
Nomenclator (1400s) — The 400-year diplomatic compromise: a small substitution alphabet plus a large code dictionary. Hall II of The Cipher Museum.
The null cipher — hide the secret in plain sight by spelling it out with the first letters of an innocuous message. Used by spies, prisoners, and Bacon, since at least the Roman empire.
One-Time Pad (Miller 1882 / Mauborgne 1917) — the only cipher mathematically unbreakable when the key is truly random, key-length, and never reused (Shannon).

Robert Patterson's 1801 four-layer transposition cipher — sent to Thomas Jefferson, who couldn't break it. Stumped American statesmen for 206 years until Lawren Smithline cracked it in 2007 using hill-climbing search.
A 1700 BCE Cretan terracotta disc stamped with 45 distinct pictograms — the world's oldest 'movable type' and one of its most enduring undeciphered scripts.
Pigpen cipher (~1700) — Freemason geometric substitution where each letter becomes the lines and dots of its grid cell. Trivial once the glyph table is seen.
Playfair cipher (1854) — Charles Wheatstone's keyed 5x5 digram cipher promoted by Lord Playfair. Used by the British in WWI; broken by digram analysis.
Polybius square (~150 BC) — ancient Greek 5x5 grid mapping each letter to a row-column digit pair. Foundation for Bifid, Trifid, Nihilist, ADFGX, and tap codes.
Porta cipher (1563) — della Porta's reciprocal polyalphabetic table where each key letter swaps two halves of the alphabet. Falls to Kasiski just like Vigenère.
Purple machine (1939) — Japan's Type 97 stepping-switch cipher for diplomatic traffic. Broken on 20 September 1940 by Frank Rowlett and the US Army SIS team.
Rail Fence cipher — write the message in a zigzag across N rails, then read off rail by rail. Trivial to break: brute-force every rail count from 2 to about 10.
The West German Red Army Faction (RAF/Baader-Meinhof) used KGB-supplied one-time pads for communications — materials discovered in 1993 after German reunification archive access.
Red (Type A) (1931-1938) - the Japanese diplomatic stepping-switch predecessor to Purple and the cryptanalytic bridge to MAGIC.
Commander Joseph Rochefort led Station HYPO and broke JN-25 in 1942, providing the intelligence that won the Battle of Midway and turned the tide of the Pacific War.
The Rosetta Stone (196 BCE) — the trilingual decree that unlocked Egyptian hieroglyphs after fourteen centuries of silence, deciphered by Champollion in 1822.
ROT13 (~1980, Usenet) — the self-inverse Caesar with shift 13, designed as a spoiler obscurer rather than a cipher. One operation toggles text in and out.
The first practical public-key cryptosystem — one key encrypts, a different key decrypts, and you can publish the encrypting key in the phone book.
Running Key cipher (19th c.) — a Vigenère variant using a long passage of natural text as the key. Broken by Friedman with high-probability-trigram dragging.

A 2nd-century Roman five-letter palindromic word square — SATOR · AREPO · TENET · OPERA · ROTAS — readable forwards, backwards, up, and down. Every element of the square also rearranges into PATER NOSTER + A and O.
Scytale (~700 BC) — the Spartan transposition device that wraps a leather strip around a rod of fixed diameter. Broken trivially by trying every rod width.
SHA-256 (2001) — a 256-bit fingerprint for any input; the verification engine of Git, Bitcoin, TLS certificates, and software integrity worldwide.
An 18th-century English garden monument bearing the cryptic letters O · U · O · S · V · A · V · V — debated for 250 years and never definitively cracked.
SIGABA (ECM Mark II) (1940) — The American WWII rotor machine the Axis never broke — fifteen rotors, irregular stepping. Hall VII of The Cipher Museum.

SIGSALY (1943–1946) was the world's first perfectly secure voice encryption system — a 50-ton machine using vinyl phonograph records as one-time pads to protect Roosevelt-Churchill phone calls during WWII.

Slidex was the British / Allied tactical paper-and-card cipher of WWII. A printed grid plus a sliding strip turned 2-letter bigrams into other bigrams. Quick at the platoon level, weak at scale — traffic analysis exploited it routinely.
Solitaire / Pontifex (1999) — Bruce Schneier's hand cipher driven by a 54-card deck (written for Cryptonomicon). Crowley showed a ~1/22.5 keystream bias.
An unidentified man found dead on an Adelaide beach in 1948 with the word 'Tamám Shud' in his pocket — and a page of letters that may or may not be a cipher.
Stager cipher (1861) — Anson Stager's Union Army route cipher that transposes whole words and salts them with code names. Never broken in the Civil War.

entries.t: Station HYPO — Pearl Harbor to Midway
entries.s: Station HYPO at Pearl Harbor was the US Navy signals intelligence unit that broke JN-25 in 1942 and gave Admiral Nimitz advance warning of the Japanese fleet's target at Midway — turning the tide of the Pacific War.
Straddling Checkerboard (1930s) — the Soviet variable-length digit substitution: common letters get one digit, rare letters two. The substitution layer of VIC.
Tap Code (1965) — the 5x5 Polybius square tapped through walls as row-then-column knocks. Used by US POWs in the Hanoi Hilton during the Vietnam War.
Trifid cipher (1902) — Felix Delastelle's three-dimensional 3x3x3 extension of the Bifid that fractionates letters into trits and shuffles them across a period.
Johannes Trithemius's progressive shift cipher (Polygraphia, 1518) — the first published polyalphabetic, where every successive letter is shifted one further than the last.
Two-Square cipher (late 19th c.) — a lighter Delastelle variant using only two keyed 5x5 squares. Many digrams self-encode, leaking the key squares.

entries.b: Never confirmed broken; far stronger than Enigma in service
entries.s: Typex (1937) — Britain's improved Enigma — five rotors, no plugboard, used at Bletchley to read its own intercepts. Hall VII of The Cipher Museum.
g: never confirmed broken; far stronger than enigma in service

entries.s: VENONA (1943–1980) was the US Army codebreaking effort that decrypted thousands of Soviet intelligence cables by exploiting key reuse in one-time pads — revealing Julius Rosenberg, Kim Philby, and the Cambridge Five.
Vernam cipher (1917) — Gilbert Vernam's AT&T XOR teleprinter patent, the direct ancestor of the One-Time Pad and every modern stream cipher including ChaCha20.
VIC cipher (1953) — Reino Häyhänen's KGB hand cipher: straddling checkerboard, double transposition, date-driven keystream. Broken in 1957 after his defection.
The Viet Minh and NLF used a system of keyed monoalphabetic substitution and prearranged signal codes during the Indochina and Vietnam Wars (1940s–1975).
Vigenère cipher (1553) — the polyalphabetic shift driven by a repeating keyword, called le chiffre indéchiffrable for 300 years. Broken by Kasiski in 1863.
Voynich Manuscript (~1400s) — a 240-page illustrated codex in an unknown script (Beinecke MS 408). Has resisted cipher and linguistic analysis for 600 years.

John Wallis of Oxford broke Royalist nomenclators for Parliament during the English Civil War, then served every English government for 50 years. Originator of professional English state cryptanalysis.
Charles Wheatstone's 1867 cryptograph — two geared clock dials whose hands sweep an outer plain alphabet and an inner mixed alphabet, generating a polyalphabetic ciphertext one click at a time.

Herbert Osborne Yardley founded America's Black Chamber in 1919, broke Japanese diplomatic codes at the 1921 Washington Naval Conference, and then infamously published the secrets in his 1931 bestseller.

The decoded German telegram of January 1917 that brought the United States into WWI. A two-stage codebook cipher (0075 then 13040), broken by Britain’s Room 40 and surfaced through one of history’s most consequential intelligence operations.
Zodiac killer ciphers (1969) — homophonic substitution as in Z-408 (broken in 1969 by the Hardens) and Z-340 (broken in 2020 by Oranchak, Eaker, Blankenship).

entries.c: Hall I · World Origins · ~1900 BCE - ~1350 CE
entries.s: World origins of cryptography from ancient Egypt and Hebrew Atbash through Greek, Roman, Indian, and Arabic traditions.
Civil War cryptography: the Stager cipher, Confederate Vigenère, and dictionary codes from the American Civil War.
Twenty-one moments when human ingenuity broke what mathematics could not. From Al-Kindi (850 AD) to the Copiale and Chaocipher reconstructions of 2010-2014.
Cryptography in art, music, literature, espionage fiction, and games — Bach's BACH motif, Poe's 'The Gold-Bug', Conan Doyle's Dancing Men, ARG ciphers, and modern puzzle hunts.
Mechanical cipher machines: Enigma, Lorenz, Jefferson Disk, and Alberti’s original cipher disk.
Military and spy ciphers used in real warfare: Nihilist, VIC, Stager, and Confederate systems.
DES, Diffie-Hellman, RSA, AES, SHA-256 — the canonical five primitives that founded modern cryptography and anchor every secure system today.
The polyalphabetic revolution: Vigenère, Beaufort, Porta, and the ciphers that defeated simple frequency analysis.
Puzzle and novelty ciphers: Pigpen, Bacon’s bilateral, tap code, and other creative encoding systems.
Classical substitution ciphers: monoalphabetic, homophonic, and Polybius square techniques that shaped cryptography for centuries.
Transposition and fractionation ciphers: rail fence, columnar, bifid, trifid, and ADFGVX systems.
One-Time Pad, Vernam cipher, VENONA, and Claude Shannon's proof of perfect secrecy — where perfect theory met operational failure.

entries.c: Hall XII · Open Problems · Living Research
entries.s: The world's most famous unbroken ciphers — Voynich, Kryptos, Beale, Dorabella, Phaistos, Shugborough, D'Agapeyeff, Somerton Man, McCormick. Open invitations to cryptanalysts.
Round a target to the nearest lattice corner — right with a short basis, wrong with a skewed one. The decoding problem beneath lattice cryptography.
A gentle first look at the elliptic-curve group law, drawn by hand, before it moves to a finite field.
Shannon’s measure of surprise: why the one-time pad is perfect and why key length is destiny.
The little theorem that makes RSA decryption undo RSA encryption. Watch a message round-trip.
Watch a smooth elliptic curve shatter into a scatter of dots over a finite field — and see why the discrete logarithm becomes hard.
Generators, order, and cyclic structure — the grammar of the discrete-log family.
The Hall of Foundations — interactive exhibits on the mathematics under cryptography: the number theory, hardness assumptions, and structures behind RSA, ECC, and the post-quantum standards.
Drag points until the curve locks and the secret intercept appears — the heart of Shamir’s Secret Sharing.
Drag a basis and hunt the shortest vector — the lattice foundation under Kyber, Dilithium, and post-quantum cryptography.
Solve for a secret vector, then switch the noise on and watch the same algebra fail — the Learning With Errors problem beneath ML-KEM and ML-DSA.
Clock arithmetic, primitive roots, and the cyclic group Diffie–Hellman lives inside.
The Ground Beneath the Curve — the modularity theorem and the number theory elliptic-curve cryptography inherits.
Multiply in a blink; factor and sweat — the one-way function, conceptual keystone of modern cryptography.
Verify a product of hidden scalars without revealing them — the bilinear pairing under zk-SNARKs.
The polynomial ring R_q = Z_q[X]/(Xⁿ+1) — the structured lattice inside ML-KEM and ML-DSA.
Why RSA can find a 2048-bit prime in moments — the Prime Number Theorem at work.

entries.t: The Random Oracle · Hall of Foundations
entries.s: Flip one input bit, scramble half the output — the idealized hash assumption beneath Fiat–Shamir signatures.
What “provably as hard as factoring” actually claims — and what it quietly assumes.
Navigate all 13 exhibit halls, the Hall of Foundations mathematics annex, and 156 exhibits in The Cipher Museum. Find your next cryptographic adventure.
Visual history of encryption from c. 1900 BC to the quantum age. Walk through 3,900+ years of codes, ciphers, and codebreakers.
Understand how classical ciphers work and how they became the foundation for modern encryption — from Caesar's shift to AES.

entries.c: Special Exhibit · The Science of Breaking Codes
entries.s: Learn how codebreakers crack ciphers. Frequency analysis, Kasiski examination, index of coincidence, and modern computational methods.
Break real ciphers. Six progressively harder challenges — from Caesar to Enigma.
Cryptography glossary: definitions of ciphers, cryptanalysis, key exchange, and encryption concepts from ancient to modern.
From AES and RSA to quantum cryptography — explore how modern encryption protects the digital world.
Compare 117 cipher systems from the 139-exhibit collection side by side. Sort by era, type, security level, hall, solved status, key method, and more.
A curated library of ciphertext challenges, known plaintexts, keys, and metadata for learning, teaching, scoring, and benchmarking classical cryptanalysis.
Paste unknown ciphertext and let the Cipher Detective walk you through the evidence — frequency analysis, Index of Coincidence, Kasiski examination — to identify the most likely cipher family.
Curated bibliography for serious students of cryptography and cryptanalysis: canonical books, academic journals, scholar profiles, and primary-source archives.
Filterable survey of cipher references in novels, television, films, and internet puzzle culture.
Teaching and overview page for the Cipher Corpus: learn about classical ciphers, cryptanalysis, and how to use the benchmark dataset.

entries.s: Track your progress through the Cipher Museum learning path. View earned badges, quiz scores, and your journey through each hall.
